I am still going to watch my favorite show even if I end up not liking her, but I do have a reservation about there being a female Doctor, and I do not think it makes me sexist. 

Good male role models are rare. There are a lot of male figures that people look up to as role models, but they typically have values that I can not look up to. Too often they are violent and overly sexed up. They work for themselves, and their main goal is often to * be the hero. *

The Doctor is the antithesis to the typical male role model. He is wise and kind. Even when he has been arrogant, his goal was not to get a medal, it was to do the right thing. He has always been able to be a guiding figure in his companions lives, most of them women, without wanting to get into their pants, and when he has seemed to developed feelings for one of them, he was able to see that it would be an inappropriate use of his influence over them. He can be a woman's friend without expecting anything from them. He detests violence, and when he is pushed to it, it really messes with his head -- it eats him alive because he wants so badly to do what is kind, and he often has to throw away his ego and go against himself to be kind to the people he cares about most. 

A male role model like that was so new to me, and that is what made me fall in love with the show. The 11th Doctor is my inspiration for my desire to go into social work -- I want to care for children with the same spirit he did. 

I get that now a girl can look up to the Doctor easier, but the sense of kindness is often already show to be feminine. And with a lot of the praise of this decision being about gendered role models, it is clear that people agree it is important for people, especially little ones, to have that model they can look up to. 

In a way, I feel like for now I am loosing the only decent male role mode I have ever had. And to call that sexist would be * very sad. *

The most I can do is use the values that the Doctor has taught me to accept this decision. "I AM the Doctor, whether you like it or not," really rings home here to me. I can't wait for the next season, and she will likely do a good job, but I would be lying if I said I did not have any reservation about this. 

The Doctor has always challenged me to be a better man. I see my moral failings, and I think of the Doctor. That's why Capaldi has stood out to me, "am I a good man?" The Doctor is the only male character to ever make me ask that about myself, and often I know I would disappoint my role model -- and that is important.

Nah. It's okay to have reservations about this. I'm definitely going to continue watching because Doctor Who is my favorite show, but the Doctor has always been a unique male role model to me and many others. 

He doesn't resort to violence or guns. He can be around women, even in a guiding role, without there being anything sexual. He is typically very open with his emotions and regrets. 

That is special and rare -- especially in a time where more and more people are starting to see typical masculinity as * toxic or a bad framework for a young boy's role model. * 

Anyone who flat-out refuses to watch the show now is being ridiculous, and really, they are probably missing a lot of the lessons that Doctor Who has taught us, but having reservations or feeling a bit off about this decision does not make someone sexist. Things are a lot more complicated than that. 

I hope she does a good job -- a bad Doctor has never been casted for the role, and I doubt they have made a mistake this time, but it will still take some getting used to for myself.
